title: AISA calls for ‘Bihar Bandh’ on July 25, against police lathi charge on protesting students

In a move to crack down on exam malpractices, the Centre has taken a slew of actions, including strengthening the anti-paper leak law and terminating services of up to 47 officials in the National Testing Agency (NTA).
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:

  • July 25, 2026 08:03
    'If Pradhan does not resign, then there is no point in this kind of meeting', says CJP national spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka

    CJP national spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka says, “...Yesterday’s meeting yielded a positive response regarding compensation and legal matters. An in-principle agreement was reached. We hope to receive that return agreement today as well. But no concrete decision has ever been made regarding the main demand, Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation. In fact, what we saw yesterday on mainstream media was that sources were saying that Pradhan will not resign. If Pradhan does not resign, then let us know; then there is no point in this kind of meeting. We will work on our future strategy... If the government continues this way, then we will be forced to opt for the tough stance.”- ANI

    Criticising new traffic advisory issued by Delhi Traffic police on Friday (July 24), CJP’s Sourav Das said, “The government wants to LAY SIEGE to Jantar Mantar!     Thousands of people continued to turn up at the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) protest at Jantar Mantar on Friday (July 24), even as the restrictions around the authorities closed the entry and exit gates at 18 metro stations, two more than were closed the previous day.     The protest’s momentum appeared undimmed despite the restrictions.

    After being criticised by several social media users for ending his hunger strike in the presence of Union Ministers, activist Sonam Wangchuk released a long video message on Friday (July 24, 2026) where he asserted that he “did not cut any deal” with the government and ended the fast as he feared a crackdown against students and protestors at Jantar Mantar.

    Read the story here,
  • July 25, 2026 06:07
    Fast-track courts for paper leak trials major step towards ensuring justice: Rekha Gupta

    Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta on Friday said setting up fast-track courts for trial in paper leak cases would be a significant step towards ensuring justice to every hard-working student.

    Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday said that the government has decided to set up fast-track courts to ensure swift and stringent punishment for those involved in paper leaks.

    In her first comment over the issue, Ms. Gupta said on X that protecting students’ interests and ensuring a bright future for the youth are the highest priorities of the government

    Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday thanked everyone for the responses and positive suggestions received to his video, where he announced the government’s decision to bring a strict law to punish those involved in paper leaks.

    In the video message, PM Modi said that a new bill incorporating provisions for strong action against paper leaks will be introduced in the ongoing session of Parliament next week.

    The draft bill, as announced by the prime minister in the Instagram video shared by him in the intervening night of Thursday and Friday, was approved by the Union Cabinet on Friday.

title: did not cut any deal with government: Sonam Wangchuk
author: Vijaita Singh
content_html:
After being criticised by several social media users for ending his hunger strike in the presence of Union Ministers, activist Sonam Wangchuk released a long video message on Friday (July 24, 2026) where he asserted that he “did not cut any deal” with the government and ended the fast as he feared a crackdown against students and protestors at Jantar Mantar. 

He said he did not press for Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan as it is inevitable due to the ongoing Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest at Jantar Mantar and movement by the youth across the country. He ended the fast around 12:30 a.m. Friday (July 24), in the presence of Union Ministers J.P. Nadda and Jitendra Singh, his wife and civil society leaders from Ladakh. Mr. Nadda served him soup to end the strike. 

“Instead, I focused on getting justice for the students and young people against whom FIRs have been registered. We saw what happened after the Ladakh incident on September 24, 2025: around 80 people were arrested and thrown in jails. For me, the future of these young people is more important. Government wasn’t ready to give a written assurance, but I refused to end my hunger strike without this key point being included in the agreement,” 

Releasing a 24:22-minute video from Medanta Hospital, where he is still under observation, Mr. Wangchuk said he wanted the members of Opposition as well as the CJP to be present, but the “agencies” did not agree. 

AFTER 26 DAYS OF HUNGER DO I NEED TO PROVE MY SINCERITY !!!
Do please watch and help spread the word. Find the full 22 minutes video on my YouTube Channel: Sonam Wangchuk pic.twitter.com/6CO3tjZsSD

— Sonam Wangchuk (@Wangchuk66) July 24, 2026

He said that even now his movement and those of his visitors has been restricted at Medanta Hospital and he is contemplating to move a contempt petition in the Delhi High Court. 

He added that he managed to ensure the presence of civil society leaders from Ladakh on Thursday (July 23) night. 

“I have lost 11 kgs, have no muscle mass. I was sitting there in heat and humidity. After 26-days of hunger strike, do I need to prove my sincerity,” he said.

title: Amarnath Yatra resumes after six-day weather halt
author: PTI
content_html:
The annual Amarnath Yatra resumed from Jammu on Saturday (July 25, 2026) after remaining suspended for six days due to inclement weather, with a fresh batch of over 6,000 pilgrims leaving the Bhagwati Nagar base camp for Baltal base camp in Kashmir Valley, officials said.

On July 19, the yatra was suspended as a precautionary measure following persistent rainfall and adverse weather conditions across Jammu and Kashmir, especially along the twin routes — traditional 48-km Pahalgam route in Anantnag district and the shorter 14-km Baltal route in Ganderbal district — to the 3,880-metre-high holy cave shrine.

Officials said the 18th batch comprising 6,269 pilgrims including 1470 women, 25 children and 54 Sadhus departed in a convoy of 223 vehicles under tight security arrangements at about 2.40 a.m. for the Baltal base camp.

No convoy was dispatched for the Pahalgam route, they said.

The pilgrimage resumed after the weather improved and the Jammu-Srinagar National Highway became trafficable again following a three-day closure triggered by landslides and shooting stones at several locations along the Udhampur-Ramban stretch, officials mentioned.

Lt. Governor Manoj Sinha flagged off the first batch of pilgrims from Bhagwati Nagar base camp on July 2, a day before the start of the annual pilgrimage in the valley.

The yatra is scheduled to conclude on August 28, coinciding with the festival of Raksha Bandhan.

So far, nearly four lakh pilgrims have visited the cave shrine, of which around 1.20 lakh pilgrims commenced their pilgrimage from the Bhagwati Nagar base camp in Jammu.

Pilgrims opting for the Jammu base camp are transported to Kashmir in escorted convoys under elaborate security arrangements.

title: More than half of the world’s migratory bird species are declining: Study
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
A new study led by researchers from Georgetown University and a collaboration of ornithologists from many global organisations, including the State of India’s Birds (SoIB) partnership, has revealed that more than half of the world’s migratory bird species are declining.

The authors of the study published in Nature Reviews Biodiversity estimate that approximately 51% of migratory bird species are declining globally across every major flyway on Earth.

Biodiversity crisis

While nearly 300 migratory species are already considered globally threatened, many once-common and widespread birds are also experiencing substantial population losses, underscoring the scale of the biodiversity crisis.

In India, this paper found that long-distance migratory birds like those that visit India from the Arctic were declining more rapidly than resident birds or shorter-distance migrants.

“The scale of the migratory bird decline is both alarming and sobering. What we’re seeing is the predictable consequence of decades of environmental degradation. Yet these declines are not inevitable. This review goes beyond documenting the crisis by identifying the major threats, highlighting the critical knowledge gaps, and providing a science-based framework for reversing declines before more species are pushed toward extinction,” said Peter P. Marra, Dean of Georgetown University’s Earth Commons Institute and co-lead author of the study.

Most visible

According to the SoIB Partnership, migratory birds are among the most visible and widespread components of global biodiversity. It said that they help regulate insect populations, disperse seeds and pollinate plants, and support food webs across ecosystems and continents.

They are also one of the primary ways people connect with nature, with millions of birdwatchers and community scientists around the world contributing observations to global databases that have become essential for understanding bird populations and informing conservation action.

“Yet understanding exactly where and why populations are declining, and which of the world’s 11,000 bird species should be considered migratory, remains a challenge,” it said.

Use of technology

It added that scientists are increasingly using advances in tracking technology, community science initiatives such as eBird, AI-enabled acoustic monitoring, and population modelling to identify migration routes, understand how populations are connected across seasons, and uncover the drivers of decline, including habitat loss, climate change, invasive species, collisions with buildings and infrastructure, disease, and pesticide use.

The authors of the study further argued that reversing declines would require conservation strategies that address these threats across entire migratory lifecycles and international flyways rather than in isolation.

“Previous analyses have brought global attention to the fact that North American and European migratory birds are declining at alarming rates. But until now, we did not have a good assessment of how birds are doing across all of the global terrestrial and marine flyways,” said Nathan W. Cooper of Smithsonian’s National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute and co-lead author of the study.

title: Tigers to be introduced in Buxa Tiger Reserve in West Bengal on October 2
author: Shiv Sahay Singh
content_html:
Tigers will be introduced in the Buxa Tiger Reserve of North Bengal on October 2, West Bengal Environment and Forest Minister Manoj Oraon said on Friday (July 24, 2025). “We are planning to introduce a tigress in Buxa Tiger Reserve on October 2,” the Minister said at an event in Kolkata.

Buxa Tiger Reserve is located in Dooars area of north Bengal, near the country’s border with Bhutan. The area was identified and15 th Tiger Reserve of the country in 1983. The reserve, with an area of 760.87 sq km stretches over a length of 50 km from west to east and 35 km from north to south.

The tiger reserve has recorded as many as, 68 species of mammals, 41 species of reptiles, more than 246 species of birds, 4 species of Amphibians along with 103 species of fishes. Earlier the tiger reserve had a good population of tigers, but the numbers of tigers have dwindled over the past few years.

Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Bhupendra Yadav in his visit to Kolkata, had said that the double-engine government was “exploring” the re-introduction of tigers in “suitable” habitats in Bengal.

Citing the successful reintroduction of tigers in Rajasthan’s Sariska, where the population has grown from zero in 2008 to 56, Mr. Yadav said a similar initiative was being planned for the “land of the Royal Bengal tiger”.

The other tiger habitat in West Bengal is Sundarban, the only mangrove ecosystem in the world that is home to Royal Bengal Tigers. There are about 100 tigers in the Sundarban and the number has remained stable over the past few years.

Senior officials of the West Bengal Forest Department said that bringing tigers to Buxa from Sundarban may not be good idea. Tigers may be introduced in Buxa from similar landscape of Assam and Bihar. The West Bengal government and National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) are considering bringing in a tigress from Valmiki Tiger Reserve of Bihar.

The NTCA protocol for re-introduction of tigers refers to an attempt to establish a tiger population in an area which was once part of its historical range, but from which it has been extirpated or become extinct. While there have been several instances of successful tiger reintroduction, the tiger reintroduction to Satkosia Tiger Reserve in Odisha had posed several challenges.

title: Tribal hamlets atop Alleri hillock in Vellore to get bitumen road soon
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
Remote tribal hamlets atop Alleri hillock, which forms part of Jawadhu Hills, on the outskirts of Vellore town will soon get their first bitumen road since Independence to reach the foothills. The District Rural Development Agency (DRDA) has sent a compensation package to Commissionerate of Land Administration of the State government for its nod to commence new road work in the hillock.

DRDA officials said that proposal to lay a bitumen road to connect tribal hamlets in the hills with plains was being pursued since 2023 after a 35-year-old tribal man, who was bitten by a snake, died on the way when he was carried on foot from the hillock to the hospital in the plains. “Continuous paperwork is being done to get clearance for the road work. Once the proposal gets its nod from the Commissionerate of Land Administration, work will start in two months,” Mohammed Wasim, Assistant Engineer (AE), DRDA, told The Hindu. 

Along with DRDA officials and M. Vijay Chandran, District Health Officer (DHO), Vellore, Collector P.S. Leela Alex inspected tribal hamlets in the hillock a few days ago. “During monsoon, hamlets in the hills are cut off from towns in the plains with sick people having to be carried by people to the nearest hospital at the foothills. A permanent bitumen road will end our ordeal,” said B. Sadaiyan, a resident.

DRDA officials said that as per plan, the new road will connect Varadalampattu and Nelli Marakollai villages, a distance of 8 km. Of the total 8 km, five kilometres of the stretch have to be laid in Alleri Reserve Forest (RF). The new stretch will help eight remote hamlets of Alleri village panchayat, which comprises 12 hamlets with a population of around 2,000 tribals.

The new road will be at least five-metre-wide. The new stretch will have at least 15 culverts to discharge excess rainwater and prevent damage to the carriageway during monsoon.

The entire work, which can be completed in six months, will cost around ₹17 crore.

Forest officials said that three hectares of forest land have been acquired for this purpose after paying a compensation of ₹1.3 crore in February. Also, six hectares of alternative land have been identified as additional compensation to the Forest Department for loss of forest land. At present, tribal hamlets in the hills only have a government primary school, a PDS outlet in a rented building, and a bike ambulance service.

DRDA officials said that as per plan, the new road will connect Varadalampattu and Nelli Marakollai villages, a distance of 8 km. Of the total 8 km, five kilometres of the stretch have to be laid in Alleri Reserve Forest (RF). The new stretch will help eight remote hamlets of Alleri village panchayat, which comprises 12 hamlets with a population of around 2,000 tribals.
The new road will be at least five-metre-wide. The new stretch will have at least 15 culverts to discharge excess rainwater and prevent damage to the carriageway during monsoon.
The entire work, which can be completed in six months, will cost around ₹17 crore.
Forest officials said that three hectares of forest land have been acquired for this purpose after paying a compensation of ₹1.3 crore in February. Also, six hectares of alternative land have been identified as additional compensation to the Forest Department for loss of forest land.  At present, tribal hamlets in the hills only have a government primary school, a PDS outlet in a rented building, and a bike ambulance service.

title: Anantnag attack aftermath: Intensify area domination, step up intelligence-led ops: J&K DGP Nalin Prabhat
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
Intensify area domination and night domination to deter anti-national elements and maintain a strong police presence, Jammu and Kashmir Director General of Police Nalin Prabhat said on Friday (July 25, 2026). 

Chairing a security review meeting at the Police Control Room, Kashmir, “to assess the prevailing security scenario and other emerging challenges across the Union Territory” in the wake of the terrorist attack at Anantnag, DGP Prabhat passed fresh directions to the top officers in Kashmir.

A police spokesman said DGP Prabhat directed the officers to intensify area domination and night domination, particularly in vulnerable and urban areas, to deter anti-national elements and maintain a strong police presence. 

He called for strengthening the security grid around critical infrastructure, “while reinforcing intelligence collection and coordination among all security and intelligence agencies”.

Reviewing the counter-terrorism framework, the DGP instructed officers to intensify intelligence-led operations to identify, track and neutralize residual terror networks. 

“The importance of close coordination among all stakeholders to facilitate swift operational responses and effectively counter any attempt to disturb public order or undermine the security environment,” said DGP Prabhat.

Highlighting the critical role of reliable communication in policing, the DGP underlined the need to ensure uninterrupted telecommunication connectivity and resilient communication networks across all police formations.

The spokesman said the DGP underlined the need “for heightened situational awareness across all formations”, while directing officers to maintain continuous oversight of weather-related preparedness. 

The spokesman said officers presented a comprehensive assessment of the prevailing security scenario across the Union Territory, including the current operational environment, threat perception and preparedness of field formations.

One policeman was killed in Anantnag two days ago in a terror attack. The policeman was shot dead from a close range by an unidentified terrorist.
